articles.title: Britons Voice Concerns Ahead of Chancellor's First Budget
articles.summary: BBC News gathered a range of citizens describing tight finances and the measures they hope the upcoming budget will address, from energy costs to housing and tax relief.
articles.content:
Chancellor John Healey is preparing to present his inaugural Budget on a Wednesday, a moment that will be closely examined as government borrowing costs sit at historic levels. The announcement comes with limited pre‑release information, prompting the Treasury to face scrutiny over its tax and spending plans.

BBC News spoke with people from different walks of life to capture how current economic pressures are affecting everyday households and what changes they would welcome from the Budget.

In south London, 40‑year‑old Chloe supports her 16‑year‑old son after the death of her husband four years ago. She benefits from a subsidised rent through a housing association, yet she notes that sharing a household would have eased her finances. Her monthly gas and electricity bill now totals about £200, and she also pays a council tax bill of a similar amount. To stretch her income, she caps her weekly grocery spend at £40 and has stopped visiting higher‑priced retailers and cinemas. "Two incomes make a massive difference," she said, highlighting the strain of relying on a single salary. Chloe does not claim benefits and works full‑time, but she urges the government to consider additional support for single‑parent families, possibly through adjustments to tax liabilities.

Robert Portlock, 29, lives with his parents in Gateshead and dreams of moving into his own flat. He estimates that a modest property would consume roughly two‑thirds of his monthly earnings, leaving little for council tax, energy, food, a TV licence, broadband, a car, and social activities. His car is essential for a 32‑mile round‑trip commute to Newcastle Airport, but the combined finance, insurance, fuel and tax costs amount to £750 each month. He advocates for a cut in fuel duty and a rise in the personal tax allowance from the current £12,570 to about £16,000. "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment," he remarked, expressing frustration with the government's 2.5 % deposit scheme for first‑time buyers.

Emily Nelson, a 19‑year‑old from Swindon, finished her A‑levels last year and has struggled to secure employment in her chosen field of animation. She is currently applying for retail, sales and apprenticeship positions but receives few responses. She calls for increased government funding for businesses to enable them to hire more young staff, as well as expanded financing for training programmes and an extension of the Jobs Guarantee scheme, which currently offers six‑month fully funded jobs to 18‑ to 24‑year‑olds on universal credit after 18 months of job‑searching. Emily hopes the eligibility period could be reduced to a year.

Professional driver Dave Herbert, 48, transports vehicles between showrooms and makes deliveries across a 62‑mile round‑trip from his home in Ynysddu to Cardiff. He reports that fuel expenses have surged, now costing him about £350 a month, representing a 40‑50 % increase from earlier in the year. He would welcome a temporary reduction or removal of fuel duty, noting that the current rate has been frozen at 57.95 pence per litre since March 2011, which he feels still places a burden on drivers.

In Essex, finance professional Jonathan Whitwam, 52, supports his two daughters through university while managing a mortgage and a household rent of roughly £18,000 a year. He anticipates his daughters graduating with substantial student‑loan debt, potentially between £45,000 and £60,000 each, with interest accruing at several thousand pounds annually. Whitwam argues for higher taxation on high earners, a one‑off wealth tax for assets over £10 million, and new levies on the oil, gas and banking sectors to fund public services such as roads, hospitals and schools.

Retired Christine Morris, 78, from Worksop lives on a state pension supplemented by a modest private pension left by her late husband. She finds it increasingly difficult to balance her finances, even as she continues to take holidays. While the prime minister has suggested removing standing charges from gas bills, Morris calls for similar relief on electricity standing charges, which tend to be higher for single occupants. She also points out that she narrowly misses eligibility for pension credit, a means‑tested benefit for pensioners receiving £238 or less per week, as she currently receives £241.

A Budget is the government's annual financial plan, outlining expected revenue and spending for the coming year. It sets the level of taxation, determines public sector investment, and can introduce new fiscal measures. Fuel duty is a tax applied to each litre of petrol or diesel sold, intended to raise revenue and influence driver behaviour; changes to its rate can affect the price at the pump. Council tax is a local levy collected by authorities to fund services such as waste collection, road maintenance and schools, calculated based on property values.

As the chancellor prepares his statements, the voices captured by BBC News illustrate a spectrum of financial pressures—from rising energy costs and housing affordability to the challenges faced by young jobseekers and retirees. Their collective input underscores the demand for targeted relief, tax adjustments, and support schemes that could ease the burden on households across the income range.

This “bet‑and‑get” structure mirrors similar offers from other national sportsbooks, where a qualifying stake triggers a set amount of bonus bets regardless of the outcome. The lack of a win condition differentiates Borgata’s offer from some competitors that only reward winning first bets.

Beyond the introductory bonus, Borgata Sportsbook provides a suite of ongoing promotions for existing users. These include daily odds boosts that raise the payout potential on selected markets at no extra cost, and a cash‑out feature that lets bettors settle a wager before the final result is known. The platform supports a wide array of sports, covering major North American leagues such as the NFL, MLB, NBA, and NHL, as well as international disciplines like soccer, tennis, and mixed martial arts. Niche markets are also represented, with betting options for Australian rules football, badminton, biathlon, boxing, cricket, cycling, darts, golf, handball, lacrosse, various motorsports, rugby, snooker, softball, table tennis, and volleyball. This breadth allows bettors to explore both mainstream and specialty events.

User experience is a central focus for Borgata. The app is optimized for quick, on‑the‑go wagering, delivering push notifications for score updates and bet results. The desktop site offers a larger view that facilitates deeper research, such as reviewing detailed statistics and managing multiple bets simultaneously.

The betting workflow follows a familiar pattern. After logging in, a user selects a desired market, adds the pick to the bet slip, enters the stake amount, and confirms the wager. For example, a bettor could choose Christopher Bell to win a NASCAR race at +1000 odds, place a $10 stake, and stand to receive $100 if the prediction is correct. The process is designed to be straightforward and intuitive.

The app integrates Borgata’s rewards program, allowing participants to earn points on each wager. Accumulated points can be redeemed for additional bonuses or perks at Borgata’s physical properties, linking the online betting experience with the brand’s broader hospitality offerings.

Performance metrics reported by the review indicate fast load times and minimal lag on both the app and the website. Secure payment options are available for deposits and withdrawals, and the platform processes transactions within the timeframes outlined in its internal reviews. Background: In sports betting, a participant selects an outcome they believe will occur and stakes money on that prediction. If the chosen outcome happens, the bettor receives a payout calculated by multiplying the stake by the odds offered at the time of the bet. Bonus bets function similarly, allowing bettors to place wagers without using their own cash, though any winnings are typically credited as bonus funds rather than withdrawable cash.

The “bet‑and‑get” model employed by Borgata is common among sportsbooks seeking to attract new users. By guaranteeing a bonus regardless of the first bet’s result, the promotion lowers the risk for newcomers and encourages them to explore the platform’s features. Competing offers from DraftKings, FanDuel, and Fanatics follow comparable structures, though the specific amounts and qualifying criteria differ.

Overall, Borgata Sportsbook presents a comprehensive betting environment tailored to New Jersey residents. The combination of an attractive welcome bonus, a broad selection of sports, user‑friendly interfaces on both mobile and desktop, and robust responsible‑gaming tools positions the service as a competitive option within the state’s regulated market.

articles.title: Neon Yellow Urine Explained: Diet, Vitamins and Kidney Health
articles.summary: Experts clarify why bright urine can appear after certain foods, supplements or medications, and when it may signal a health issue.
articles.content:
According to reporting by The Guardian, a physician who advises several members of the Trump administration has praised a diet of meat and fermented foods for producing urine that looks like the soft drink Mountain Dew. The comment sparked interest in how diet and other factors influence urine colour and what the shade might reveal about health.

Urine normally appears yellow because of a pigment called urobilin, which is generated by gut bacteria as they break down hemoglobin. The concentration of this pigment determines the shade: more water dilutes the colour, making it lighter, while dehydration or reduced fluid intake yields a darker hue. This basic relationship means that urine is often deeper in the morning or after periods of low fluid consumption.

Experts caution that colour charts that assign specific shades to health states are imprecise. “they are considered imprecise,” says Suzanne Watnick, a nephrologist at the University of Washington, adding that clinicians do not rely on such charts for serious decisions such as managing kidney disease. For most individuals, thirst is a more reliable guide to hydration than the colour of urine, although people who must stay highly hydrated, such as those prone to kidney stones, may aim for very pale urine as a practical indicator.

The kidneys continuously filter blood to remove excess water, waste products, minerals, salts and acid, delivering the filtered fluid to the bladder for excretion. This process maintains a stable internal environment. “Your kidneys are really smart,” notes Sharon Moe, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine, emphasizing that healthy kidneys regulate fluid balance automatically and that excess water‑soluble nutrients are expelled in the urine.

Certain foods and supplements can alter urine colour beyond the usual yellow. B‑vitamin supplements, especially riboflavin, can produce a fluorescent yellow that resembles a neon hue. Rhubarb may lend a reddish‑brown tint, while beets can create a pinkish shade. In contrast, consuming large amounts of beef tends to make urine more acidic without changing its colour. The bright neon shade described by the Trump‑linked doctor is consistent with the effect of high intake of water‑soluble vitamins.

When an unexpected colour appears, the first step is to review any recent supplement use and discontinue them temporarily. If the urine returns to a normal shade, the supplement is likely the cause. If the colour persists, the next step is to eliminate brightly coloured foods from the diet. A review of current medications is also advisable, as some prescribed drugs can change urine colour as a harmless side effect. However, patients should not stop taking prescribed medicines without consulting a clinician.

More serious colour changes, such as persistent red or brown urine, warrant medical evaluation, especially if accompanied by new pain, rash, severe leg swelling, or other concerning symptoms. These signs can indicate bleeding in the kidneys, bladder or urinary tract, which clinicians can assess with a simple urine test. In menstruating individuals, distinguishing menstrual blood from urinary blood may require additional clarification from a health professional.

Foamy urine can be a sign of protein leakage from the kidneys. While occasional bubbles are normal, a froth that resembles the head of a beer may indicate a problem. Changes in odor, frequency of urination, and clarity are also relevant; a sweet or foul smell, a marked increase or decrease in voiding, or cloudy urine should prompt a check‑up.

Kidney disease often progresses without obvious symptoms. In the United States, 37 million adults have chronic kidney disease, yet only one in ten are aware of their condition. Prevention strategies highlighted by experts include maintaining healthy blood pressure, consuming a diet rich in fruits and vegetables, and limiting meat intake. “The carnivore diet is not a healthy diet,” Moe states, underscoring the importance of balanced nutrition for kidney health.

Overall, neon‑yellow urine is generally harmless for people with normal kidney function and is most often linked to the intake of certain vitamins or brightly coloured foods. Monitoring hydration through thirst, being aware of supplement and medication effects, and seeking medical advice for persistent or symptomatic colour changes remain the recommended approach.

articles.title: United’s Crisis Deepens as Carrick Faces Uncertain Future
articles.summary: Manchester United’s recent defeat and internal clash between manager Michael Carrick and captain Bruno Fernandes have intensified calls for change, with the club hovering near the relegation zone.
articles.content:
Manchester United manager Michael Carrick left the Old Trafford pitch on Sunday to a chorus of his name from the home crowd, a moment that may mark the end of his tenure on the sidelines. The applause came after a 3-0 loss to Bournemouth, a result that has been described as a 40‑year low for the club and has left United just a point above the relegation zone. The defeat was United’s sixth of the season and the team has now gone eight matches without a win in any competition.

The opening seven league games this campaign constitute United’s worst start since 1986, and the latest setback deepened a slide that has seen the club hover precariously close to the bottom of the table. Fans, traditionally known for their loyalty, used the post‑match moments to send a clear signal to the dressing room, directing their frustration through the figure of captain Bruno Fernandes, who remained an unused substitute.

Fernandes, the Professional Footballers’ Association’s Player of the Year last season, was left out of the squad after publicly criticizing Carrick following a 4-1 defeat to Como in the UEFA Champions League. Since arriving in 2020, the Portuguese midfielder has been a fan favourite, earning a reputation as a club legend after helping United secure a third‑place finish and recording a record number of assists in a Premier League season. His omission from the Bournemouth match was widely interpreted as a direct response to his earlier remarks about the team’s tactics.

The Premier League is England’s top football division, where clubs compete over a season for the championship and European qualification. Performance in the league determines a club’s standing, with the bottom teams facing relegation to a lower division. Success in the competition is a key measure of a club’s health and prestige.

Carrick’s rise to the permanent role began after an interim spell that saw him replace Ruben Amorim in January of the previous season. His short‑term impact was positive enough to earn a full‑time appointment in the summer, but the current run of results suggests that his tenure may be reaching its limit. The growing rift between the manager and Fernandes, who publicly questioned the tactical approach that failed to break down Italian opposition, has intensified speculation about who will ultimately bear responsibility.

Historically, United supporters have rarely expressed discontent with managers or players, with boos being a relatively recent phenomenon. This season, however, the atmosphere at Old Trafford has shifted dramatically. While the crowd sang Carrick’s name as he exited the pitch, the same supporters also used the captain’s bench as a conduit for their displeasure, sending a message that the internal discord cannot be ignored.

"Manchester United need to make the change tonight," former England teammate Jamie Carragher told Sky Sports when asked whether a sacking was warranted. Carragher argued that the fans’ support for Carrick stemmed more from his historical connection to the club than from his current results, and he warned that the situation had become untenable for both the manager and the captain.

In the post‑match press conference, Carrick accepted responsibility for the team’s position. "I take the responsibility," he said, adding that he understood the situation and was not expecting any particular outcome. He expressed mixed emotions about the fans’ reaction, noting that the respect shown by supporters meant a great deal to him. "I always do what I feel is going to be the best for the club, whatever decision is made," he continued, emphasizing his commitment to the club regardless of future developments.

Former United defender Gary Neville, while not quoted directly, has suggested that Carrick’s popularity with fans does not necessarily translate to support from the owners, the sporting department, or the playing group. Neville implied that a decision may be forthcoming that could disappoint supporters but might be deemed necessary by the club’s hierarchy.

United’s history is marked by periods of rebuilding and resurgence. The club endured a low point in 1990 when Sir Alex Ferguson, then the most successful manager in its history, was reportedly close to being dismissed before leading the team to an FA Cup triumph and a subsequent era of sustained success. Earlier, a long title drought that stretched from 1967 to 1994 was broken after the signing of Eric Cantona, sparking a period of dominance that cemented United’s status as a global football powerhouse.

The current season finds United at a crossroads, with the gap to the relegation zone appearing increasingly realistic. Their cross‑town rivals, Manchester City, are also facing a challenging campaign, raising the spectre that both Manchester clubs could be threatened by relegation. The internal power struggle between Carrick and Fernandes, highlighted by the captain’s criticism of the team’s pressing strategy, suggests that any managerial change may be driven more by dressing‑room dynamics than by fan sentiment alone.

As the club navigates this precarious phase, the next steps will likely be decided by the owners and senior sporting officials. The combination of poor results, a strained relationship between manager and captain, and mounting pressure from supporters creates a volatile environment. Whether Carrick will remain at the helm or be relieved of his duties remains uncertain, but the situation underscores the depth of United’s current challenges.

The reporting on this development comes from Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Wonder Targets Texas Expansion and IPO Amid Automation Push
articles.summary: Marc Lore's Wonder, valued at $9 billion, plans a Texas rollout, a subscription model for user-built eateries, and a possible IPO, while pursuing full kitchen automation by 2040.
articles.content:
Wonder, the food‑service startup founded by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, has quickly grown from a concept of mobile kitchens to a network of brick‑and‑mortar locations that combine multiple restaurant brands under one roof. The company describes itself as a platform that brings together the best eateries from across the United States, allowing customers to order takeout or delivery through its own app or third‑party services such as Grubhub, which Wonder now owns. Lore told CNBC that "Wonder is a vertically integrated food technology platform to make great food more accessible." The model aims to keep menu prices below the cost of delivered groceries by eliminating delivery fees for app users and avoiding commission‑based price inflation.

The business plan hinges on a nationwide rollout that includes urban, suburban and rural sites, with a particular focus on exurban areas where dining options are limited. Wonder’s storefronts are fully electric and require no gas lines or venting, a design choice that speeds up site acquisition and reduces renovation hurdles. Food is prepared in central commissary kitchens, then shipped to each location where staff finish cooking and serve the dishes. The menu draws from more than two dozen partner concepts, ranging from Indian street food to barbecue, and includes collaborations with celebrity chefs who receive upfront payments and equity stakes.

Automation is a core pillar of Lore’s long‑term vision. The company is already using robots to assemble salads, bowls, sauces and beverages, and it has set a target of fully autonomous food preparation and delivery by 2040. To fund this ambitious roadmap, Wonder has raised $3.3 billion from investors that include DoorDash, Alphabet’s venture arm GV and actress‑entrepreneur Gwyneth Paltrow. A recent Series D round pushed its pre‑money valuation to $9 billion, a figure comparable to the sale price of a major sandwich chain two years earlier.

In addition to scaling its physical footprint, Wonder is experimenting with a subscription‑based service called Wonder Create, slated to launch on November 17. For a $10 monthly fee, influencers, entrepreneurs or brands can set up a “restaurant” inside an existing Wonder location and earn a share of the revenue. Artificial intelligence will assist participants in crafting a brand identity, pricing strategy and recipe lineup, effectively lowering the barriers to restaurant ownership.

Another AI‑driven initiative, the MEL platform, can integrate personal health data—from wearable devices to blood biomarkers—to generate personalized meal plans. Although MEL is not yet available to customers, Lore uses the technology for his own meals, illustrating the company’s broader ambition to blend nutrition science with on‑demand food.

Background: A vertically integrated food platform controls multiple stages of the supply chain, from sourcing ingredients to final delivery, allowing tighter cost management and consistent quality. Food halls aggregate several dining concepts in a single space, offering consumers variety without the need to travel between separate establishments.

Wonder’s growth strategy includes a major push into Texas, where the company plans to open at least 100 locations by the end of 2027. This expansion follows the opening of 170 storefronts across states from Virginia to Massachusetts over the past three years. The Texas rollout is seen as a test of the model in a large, diverse market that blends urban centers with sprawling suburbs.

The company’s acquisition spree has exceeded $1 billion, encompassing Grubhub, logistics firm Relay, meal‑kit provider Blue Apron and several New York‑based restaurant concepts. These purchases have broadened Wonder’s capabilities in delivery, supply chain management and brand portfolio, though they have also contributed to ongoing financial losses.

Despite the aggressive expansion, Wonder faces scrutiny from consumers and analysts. Social‑media feedback has highlighted mixed experiences, with some diners describing the food as average and price points higher than expected. Lore emphasized that the startup collects thousands of daily reviews rating taste, temperature and portion size, and that board meetings begin with a review of these scores. He noted, "We’re maniacally focused on food quality .... We're constantly iterating on the meals that score lower, and see over time, the last 12 months, our taste scores have improved, our Google reviews have improved."

Industry observers point out that Wonder’s model differs from the ghost‑kitchen phenomenon that surged during the pandemic. While ghost kitchens operate without dine‑in space and have struggled as delivery volumes receded, Wonder maintains a physical front‑of‑house where customers can sit and eat. This hybrid approach is intended to combine the efficiency of centralized cooking with the customer experience of a traditional restaurant.

Investor interest remains strong, partly due to Lore’s track record of building and exiting e‑commerce ventures. He previously co‑founded Diapers.com, which sold to Amazon for $545 million, and later launched Jet.com, acquired by Walmart for about $3 billion. His experience in scaling online businesses is viewed as a valuable asset for Wonder’s technology‑driven ambitions.

The prospect of an initial public offering is a recurring theme in recent discussions. Lore has indicated that going public would provide capital for further expansion and a public currency for future acquisitions, though he declined to specify a timeline. In March, Wonder appointed Gabrielle Scheibe Rabinovitch, formerly of Worldpay, as chief financial officer to steer the company through the IPO preparation process.

Analysts caution that the broader market environment for high‑growth, unprofitable startups has tightened. To attract public‑market investors, Wonder will need to demonstrate a clear path toward profitability, whether through cost reductions from automation, higher customer retention, or successful monetization of its subscription services.

Overall, Wonder’s blend of technology, brand aggregation and ambitious geographic expansion positions it as a notable contender in the evolving food‑service landscape. The company’s next steps—Texas rollout, Wonder Create launch, and potential IPO—will test whether its vertically integrated model can deliver consistent quality and value at scale, as reported by CNBC.

articles.title: Manchester United Women Revamp Tactics to Reverse Early Season Slump
articles.summary: After a winless start, United have won six straight games, climbing to fifth and preparing for a derby with City, thanks to tactical tweaks and renewed team cohesion, BBC Sport reports.
articles.content:
Manchester United’s women’s side entered the new season struggling to find form, but a series of adjustments have sparked a revival as they prepare to face league leaders Manchester City in a highly anticipated derby. The team arrived at the start of the campaign without a victory and with confidence visibly low after three opening league fixtures that failed to deliver points.

A breakthrough arrived in the Women’s League Cup when United secured a win over Sheffield United, marking the beginning of a six‑match winning streak that now stretches across all competitions. This run has lifted the club to fifth place in the league table, leaving them eight points behind the unbeaten City side they are set to meet on Sunday.

Manager Eva Olid, who took charge in the summer, has identified several key changes that have turned the tide. Early on, her philosophy of dominant possession, an aggressive attacking outlook and a high‑risk approach proved difficult for the squad to execute, resulting in limited shots and low possession percentages in defeats to London City Lionesses and Chelsea. Recognising the need to balance new ideas with existing strengths, Olid urged her players to return to the defensive solidity they displayed before a 1‑1 draw with Arsenal, while gradually layering in elements of her preferred style. She explained, "The things they were good at before, they need to keep and at the same time, little by little, we need to implement our new style." 

The stalemate against Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium served as a catalyst, providing a platform for further improvement. Following that match, United faced a sequence of games against lower‑ranked opponents, all played at home, and the contrast in performance was stark. The side collected the full nine points available, found the net six times while conceding only twice, and saw a noticeable rise in possession rates.

Statistical indicators underline the shift. In the first three league outings the team managed just 197 passes that reached the final third; that figure swelled to a combined 529 across the subsequent fixtures against West Ham, Liverpool and Charlton Athletic. Shot creation also surged, with attempts climbing from ten in the early period to forty‑two in the later matches, and United began to win a greater share of aerial duels.

Off the pitch, the club navigated a "transitional period" after a heavy 5‑0 loss to Chelsea, prompting candid discussions aimed at rebuilding confidence. Olid highlighted the importance of these conversations, noting that they helped clarify what the players required from her and what she expected in return. She later reflected on the break in international play as an opportunity to restructure the coaching team, stating, "I had time to re‑organise everything, the roles for the new staff and how we are going to work together." The pause was described as a fresh start that retained positive energy while establishing new foundations.

Individual performances also began to improve. Vice‑captain Ella Toone, who missed an England call‑up for the first time under Sarina Wiegman, responded by scoring in a 3‑1 victory over Charlton. Summer signing Andrea Medina has emerged as an essential component of the squad, and England defender Maya le Tissier returned from the international break with renewed vigor after impressing for her country.

The backroom staff saw reinforcement as well, with fellow Spaniard Jose Herrera joining as assistant coach and Gavin Beith, a former colleague from Hearts, also taking up an assistant role. These appointments have contributed to a more cohesive environment that Olid hopes will sustain future success.

Background: The Women's Super League represents the top tier of English women's football, featuring a season where clubs compete for the championship and qualification for European competition. Derbies, such as the clash between Manchester United and Manchester City, carry additional significance due to local rivalry and often serve as pivotal moments that can influence a team's momentum.

Looking ahead, United view the upcoming derby as an extra source of motivation. Olid emphasized that big games are used to boost confidence while also providing a specific challenge, noting that the rivalry itself already fuels player enthusiasm. The team aims to carry the confidence built over the recent winning run into the match, hoping to test their renewed balance against the league leaders.

United’s resurgence demonstrates how tactical flexibility, reinforced defensive organization, and clear communication within the squad can reverse an early‑season slump. As they approach the high‑stakes encounter with City, the focus remains on maintaining the blend of established strengths and the gradual introduction of Olid’s vision, a strategy that has already yielded tangible improvements, according to BBC Sport.

articles.title: Labour explores four tax routes to fund budget without raising income tax
articles.summary: BBC News outlines four potential revenue measures Labour could use to rebuild the Treasury’s cash buffer while keeping income tax, VAT and NI unchanged.
articles.content:
The chancellor’s "headroom" – the cash buffer that helps the government meet fiscal rules and limit borrowing – has been under pressure, with economists estimating it may have fallen from around £24bn to as low as £11bn in recent months. Restoring that buffer is a key objective for the upcoming Budget, and Labour’s 2024 election manifesto has pledged not to increase income tax, VAT or National Insurance rates.

Background: "Headroom" refers to the amount of fiscal space a government has before it must take action to stay within its own spending limits. When the buffer shrinks, the Treasury must either cut spending or find new revenue sources to avoid breaching its rules.

One avenue under discussion is raising the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax. Tax Policy Associates estimates that increasing the surcharge from 3% to 5.5% could generate an additional £1bn to £2bn each year. The higher levy would cut the profits banks can distribute to shareholders, potentially affecting wealthy investors and, indirectly, ordinary savers whose pension funds hold bank shares. Research suggests banks might shift part of the burden onto customers through lower savings rates or higher borrowing costs.

Background: The corporation tax surcharge is an extra percentage added to the standard corporate tax rate for banks, intended to reflect the stability they provide to the financial system. Adjusting the surcharge changes the overall tax bill paid by banking institutions.

A second proposal targets electronic gaming machines found in betting shops and adult gaming centres. Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown has urged the chancellor to increase the tax on these machines, which can pay out up to £500 per game. The Social Market Foundation estimates that doubling the tax from 20% to 40% could raise between £275m and £460m annually, depending on how gamblers respond. Critics warn that the extra cost could be passed to players through poorer odds, while the gambling industry argues it could force betting shops to close, threatening jobs in related sectors such as horse racing.

The third measure focuses on online marketplaces. The Treasury says it loses about £12bn a year in VAT revenue because some sellers on platforms like Amazon, eBay and Temu fail to comply with VAT rules. By making the platforms responsible for collecting VAT from retailers using their services, the government hopes to close part of the "VAT tax gap". Analysts suggest the change could bring in roughly £1bn a year, with Amazon itself estimating a possible £700m contribution.

Together, the bank surcharge increase, the gambling machine tax hike and the online‑marketplace VAT collection could raise a maximum of around £3.5bn annually. While this would help rebuild the chancellor’s cash buffer, it remains a modest sum compared with the broader fiscal challenges.

Labour also faces pressure to fund rising living costs and defence spending, all while adhering to its pledge not to raise the main consumption taxes. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called for a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK’s welfare bill, and opposition parties are urging savings from working‑age benefits. The Conservatives claim they could save £36bn a year by tightening welfare access, and Reform suggests £50bn could be saved, though independent analysts question the realism of such large cuts.

Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic, with the Office for Budget Responsibility projecting the cost to climb from £68bn this year to £81bn by 2031. Labour leaders Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves previously sought to trim £5bn from these benefits by 2030, but a revolt among backbench MPs forced a reversal. Experts note that any genuine savings in the working‑age welfare budget would likely require upfront investment to help claimants move into employment, which could offset immediate Treasury gains.

The debate over how to restore the Treasury’s headroom illustrates the tension between fiscal prudence and the political commitment to protect low‑ and middle‑income households from higher taxes. As the Budget approaches, the chancellor will need to balance these competing demands while delivering the revenue needed to meet the government’s borrowing targets and fund priority spending.

articles.title: Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts blood clot draws criticism from NFL peers
articles.summary: Jalen Hurts was sidelined after blood clots were discovered in his lungs, prompting scrutiny of the Philadelphia Eagles' medical decisions and comments from fellow players, while the league says protocols were followed.
articles.content:
Philadelphia quarterback Jalen Hurts was placed on the inactive list indefinitely after doctors identified blood clots in both of his lungs. The discovery followed a series of medical evaluations that began with a superficial clot found in his calf during a team walk‑through before the Eagles' Week 5 game in London. Despite that finding, Hurts played the contest against the Jacksonville Jaguars and then returned to the United States on the team flight. Subsequent testing after the trip revealed a deep‑vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, injuries that are expected to keep him out for the remainder of the regular season.

The National Football League reviewed the sequence of events and concluded that the procedures leading to Hurts' participation in the London matchup were handled appropriately. The league’s assessment emphasizes that the established medical protocols were observed, even as the situation continues to generate discussion among players, officials and the players’ union. The NFL Players Association, however, has formally requested a deeper investigation into the handling of the case, indicating that the union believes additional scrutiny is warranted.

Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III, who dealt with blood clots in his own lungs while in high school, offered his perspective during a Friday press conference. "Yeah, honestly, just stay positive," Walker said, adding that he would be praying for Hurts and urging the quarterback to follow all necessary steps to recover his health. Walker’s comments highlighted concerns shared by many about the risks of air travel for an athlete with a clotting condition and underscored the seriousness with which he views the situation.

Blood clots such as deep‑vein thrombosis can form in the deep veins of the legs and may travel to the lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism. The condition is medically serious because it can impair oxygen exchange and strain the cardiovascular system. Treatment typically involves anticoagulant medication and, in some cases, procedures to remove or dissolve the clot. Athletes with this diagnosis are generally advised to avoid activities that could exacerbate the clot, including long flights, until cleared by medical professionals.

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers, who has previously expressed disagreements with the league’s medical staff, also weighed in on the matter. "We're in the quarterback fraternity, so you don't want to see anything like that happen to anybody," Rodgers said, noting that he was not surprised by the confusion surrounding the Eagles' handling of Hurts. He referenced his own limited knowledge of the specifics while acknowledging ongoing tensions with the NFL’s chief medical officer.

The quarterback fraternity refers to the informal network of NFL signal‑callers who often share insights about health, preparation and the pressures of the position. Within this community, concerns about medical transparency and player safety are common, especially when a high‑profile athlete faces a life‑threatening condition. The NFL’s medical office, led by the director of medical affairs, is responsible for setting league‑wide health standards, but individual teams also retain authority over day‑to‑day medical decisions for their players.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell responded to the NFLPA’s request by stating that he welcomes a thorough investigation but reaffirmed that the league’s protocols were followed in Hurts’ case. He emphasized that the primary focus is the quarterback’s health and future, describing Hurts as a young man whose well‑being is a priority for the league and its members.

With Hurts unavailable, the Eagles have turned to backup quarterback Tanner McKee to lead the offense. McKee, who was on the roster as a rookie, is now expected to assume the starting role while the team navigates the remainder of the season without its primary signal‑caller.

The episode has sparked a broader conversation about how teams assess medical risks, especially when travel and competition schedules intersect with serious health concerns. While the league maintains that its procedures were correctly applied, the union’s call for further review reflects ongoing tension between player safety advocates and organizational protocols.

CBS Sports reported on the reactions from Walker and Rodgers, as well as the statements from league officials, providing a snapshot of the current debate surrounding the Eagles’ management of the situation. The continued absence of Hurts leaves Philadelphia to adjust its game plan and underscores the unpredictable nature of health issues in professional sports.

As the investigation proceeds, the focus remains on ensuring that medical decisions prioritize player welfare while balancing the competitive demands of the NFL season. The outcome may influence future guidelines for handling similar cases, particularly those involving clotting disorders and the risks associated with long‑distance travel.

articles.title: Funding Pull Threatens Belfast Haematology Centre for Cancer Care
articles.summary: The Department of Health withdrew £1.5 million from a Belfast haematology project, delaying its opening to 2031 and raising concerns over patient safety, according to Belfast Health Trust officials.
articles.content:
The Belfast Health and Social Care Trust’s plan to create a dedicated haematology centre for cancer patients has been jeopardised after the Northern Ireland Department of Health removed a portion of its financial support, the trust’s chief executive said. The decision was criticised as "disgraceful" during a health committee meeting at Stormont.

The proposed unit was intended to be built on the Belfast City Hospital site, requiring the relocation of roughly 80 staff members from the current ward to free up space. The trust had scheduled the move as part of a broader effort to provide specialised care for patients with blood‑related cancers.

During the committee session, officials disclosed that the Department of Health had decided to retract £1.5 million previously allocated for the decanting phase of the project. The withdrawal was linked to concerns over the trust’s appraisal of options and the robustness of the capital cost estimate, according to the chief executive.

The department responded that it would continue to fund the majority of the additional expenses and would collaborate with the trust to manage rising costs associated with capital projects. A spokesperson indicated that the trust should cover one element of the scheme, estimated at around £1.05 million, from its general capital allocation over the next two years.

The overall budget for the haematology centre has more than doubled, climbing from an initial estimate of £8 million to a current projection of £19 million. The Department of Health highlighted this escalation as a factor in its decision to pull the £1.5 million, while also noting that the trust receives a substantial portion of the executive’s budget.

Jennifer Welsh, chief executive of the Belfast Trust, said the relocation of the staff remains a significant hurdle. She warned that the funding shortfall could pose a "substantial risk" to the project’s timeline and that the matter had been escalated to the permanent secretary of the Department of Health for further review.

Democratic Unionist Party assembly member Diane Dodds expressed concern that patients currently occupy inadequate conditions within the city hospital, lacking proper isolation for those with severely compromised immune systems. She described the proposed haematology unit as a source of hope for cancer patients in Northern Ireland and urged swift action to avoid further delays.

Alliance Party assembly member Nuala McAllister also criticised the funding decision, calling it "disgraceful". She highlighted that the patients affected are undergoing intensive treatments and rely on highly specialised staff, emphasizing that the department’s refusal to release the £1.5 million endangers some of the most immuno‑compromised cancer patients.

Haematology units focus on diagnosing and treating blood cancers such as leukaemia and lymphoma. Because patients receiving chemotherapy or stem‑cell transplants often have weakened immune systems, these facilities are designed with isolation rooms and strict infection‑control measures to protect vulnerable individuals.

Capital projects in the health sector are typically financed through a mix of government allocations and internal trust budgets. When projected costs rise, trusts may be asked to absorb part of the expense from their general capital plans, which are spread over several years to manage cash flow.

The withdrawal has pushed the anticipated opening of the haematology centre back by a year, with the new target now set for March 2031. The trust continues to explore alternative financing options for moving the staff and hopes to secure the remaining resources needed to complete the facility.

Both political parties and health officials stressed that delays could leave immunocompromised patients at increased risk, underscoring the urgency of resolving the funding dispute. The situation remains under close scrutiny as the Department of Health and the Belfast Trust work toward a resolution, according to reporting by BBC News.

The trust has indicated that, while it seeks additional funding, it will maintain existing services for haematology patients within the current hospital layout. Interim measures include enhanced infection‑control protocols and the allocation of dedicated staff to support those undergoing treatment, aiming to mitigate any adverse effects until the new centre becomes operational.

articles.title: Congo Confirms Ebola Outbreak Has Spread to an Eighth Province
articles.summary: Two cases, including one death, were confirmed in North Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic, as the outbreak passes 9,400 cases.
articles.content:
Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo have confirmed that the country's Ebola outbreak has spread to an eighth province, extending an epidemic that officials describe as the worst in the nation's history. The National Institute for Biomedical Research announced on Sunday, October 18, that two cases, including one death, had been confirmed in North Ubangi, a province in the far north that borders the Central African Republic, according to Reuters.

The announcement followed earlier reporting. Reuters said on Thursday that two cases had been confirmed in the province, citing two health officials, at a time when Congolese authorities had not yet made a public statement. Sunday's confirmation made the spread official and added a new region to an outbreak that health workers have been struggling to contain.

The Health Ministry said both patients are men in their 20s who live in the Wapinda health zone, which sits next to Bas-Uele province, where Ebola cases have already been reported. A health official in North Ubangi told Reuters that a series of suspected deaths had recently occurred in a mining area in Wapinda, and that samples from the area were being tested at a provincial laboratory.

The newly affected province joins seven others: North Kivu, Ituri, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and South Ubangi. The outbreak remains concentrated in eastern Congo. Ituri province is still the epicentre and accounts for almost three quarters of confirmed cases, according to the government's most recent data, while cases have also been rising in North Kivu. Across the country, 66 health zones have been affected since the outbreak began.

The latest national situation report gives a sense of the scale. In the 24 hours to October 16, Congo recorded 67 new confirmed cases and 26 new deaths. That brought the cumulative total since the outbreak began to 9,415 cases and 4,536 deaths. Of the 67 new cases, 44 were in Ituri.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus and was announced in mid-May. Reuters describes it as the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, and the Associated Press reports that it is the deadliest in Congo's history. Bundibugyo has no approved vaccine or treatment, which limits the tools available to responders and places more weight on measures such as finding the contacts of infected people, isolating patients and arranging safe burials.

The virus has also crossed Congo's borders. Cases have been recorded in Uganda, which had been declared free of Ebola in August, and in Kenya, where seven infections have been confirmed this month. Kenya announced its first case earlier in October.

The World Health Organization's regional director for Africa, Mohamed Yakub Janabi, told the Associated Press during a visit to Beni in eastern Congo that the picture is mixed. In his assessment, individual pockets of the outbreak are generally declining, but the disease is spreading out geographically. Officials and aid groups point to several factors behind the spread, including large movements of people, violence by armed rebel groups, mistrust of health workers in some communities, and poor working conditions for front-line staff.

Authorities in North Kivu province are also acting to slow transmission. Congo's state news agency ACP reported on Sunday that the province will introduce a one-week ban from Monday on people entering from Ituri.

As general background, Ebola disease is a severe illness that spreads through direct contact with the body fluids of infected people or with contaminated materials. That is why response teams concentrate on tracing everyone who has been in contact with a confirmed case, and why sudden clusters of unexplained deaths, such as those reported in the Wapinda mining area, are treated as signals that need laboratory testing quickly.

The confirmation in North Ubangi puts a province on the border with another country on the list of affected areas. The Health Ministry has so far reported only the two confirmed cases there, and the figures released do not show how many other people may have been exposed.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV Returns to the Vatican Four Days After Lung Cancer Surgery
articles.summary: The 71-year-old pontiff left Rome's Gemelli Hospital after surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung; doctors describe his condition as satisfactory.
articles.content:
Pope Leo XIV returned to the Vatican on Saturday, October 17, four days after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. The 71-year-old pontiff left Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital shortly after 3:30 p.m. local time and was driven to the Vatican, entering through the Porta del Perugino and going back to his apartment in the Apostolic Palace, according to reports from EWTN News, Reuters and the Italian news agency ANSA.

Leo had been admitted to the hospital the previous Tuesday. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung to extract the tumour. Reuters reported that he was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis came in the 17th month of the Chicago-born pope's papacy; he was elected in May 2025. The news rattled the Vatican and the world's 1.4 billion Catholics for several days.

Doctors cleared him to leave after reviewing his blood tests, a chest X-ray taken that morning and his overall clinical condition, according to a Vatican medical bulletin. The two physicians overseeing his treatment, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, formally signed off on the discharge. Margaritora told Vatican News that the pope's condition was entirely satisfactory and said he expected about ten more days before the pontiff would be fully recovered.

Footage and photos from the departure showed the pope in good spirits. He walked on foot across the hospital lobby, shook hands, waved and spoke briefly with the doctors and hospital officials who had treated him. Daniele Franco, the chairman of the Gemelli hospital foundation, was among those who welcomed him as he left. Before getting into the car, Leo greeted members of the public who had gathered along the barriers, some of whom handed him gifts.

One exchange drew particular attention. The pope stopped to speak with Varvara Struck, a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl who survived cancer and had come to wish him well, AFP reported. She had told the agency earlier in the day that she hoped her positive energy would help him recover quickly. ANSA noted that Leo raised his right arm, the side of the operated lung, as he greeted the crowd, and that he did not appear tired.

The discharge followed a steady recovery in hospital. The Vatican released the first images of the pope after surgery on Friday, showing him presiding at Mass in a room that had been set up on the hospital's tenth floor because the Gemelli chapel is under renovation. He had resumed some work on Thursday and, in the days after the operation, met with senior Vatican officials, including Archbishop Paolo Rudelli of the Secretariat of State and Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, according to EWTN News. Doctors said on Friday that his tests showed steady improvement.

Messages of support came from Italy's leadership. President Sergio Mattarella sent his warmest wishes for a peaceful convalescence and a speedy, complete recovery on behalf of the country and himself.

The pope cancelled all of his audiences until October 20. On Sunday, he appeared before thousands of people in St. Peter's Square for the Angelus prayer and thanked everyone who had prayed for him during his hospitalization. He singled out the doctors, nurses and staff of the hospital for particular gratitude and said that he would gradually resume his usual duties following the surgery, the Associated Press reported.

Local reports have said that a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17 remains on the papal calendar. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's Secretary of State, was quoted as saying that the pope may need to adjust his pace according to his health, and he described the first post-surgery photograph as an encouraging sign.

As general background, adenocarcinoma is a type of cancer that starts in glandular cells, and surgery to remove the affected part of the lung is a standard treatment for lung tumours that can be operated on. The Vatican has presented the operation and the discharge as steps in a recovery that will now continue at home, where the pope is expected to rest while gradually returning to his work.

articles.title: Brewers and Rays Meet in World Series With a First-Time Champion Guaranteed
articles.summary: Milwaukee, the NL champion with MLB's best record, faces Tampa Bay in a series that will crown a franchise's first title.
articles.content:
The Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays are meeting in the 2026 World Series, a matchup that guarantees baseball a first-time champion. Neither franchise has ever won the title. Game 1 was scheduled for Friday, October 23, at American Family Field in Milwaukee, in the 122nd edition of the Fall Classic. This article previews the series and does not report on the results of any games.

The Brewers arrive as the National League champions and the owners of the best record in baseball, 103-59, which gave them home-field advantage. They reached the World Series for the first time since 1982 after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers, the back-to-back defending champions, in the NL Championship Series. Milwaukee went 7-1 in the postseason leading into the World Series, with six comeback wins, and won all four of its home playoff games. Because of a first-round bye and the sweep in the NLCS, the Brewers had more than a week off between the end of the Dodgers series and the start of the World Series.

The Rays won the American League pennant with a 7-3 victory over the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the ALCS on Monday night at Tropicana Field. Cleveland had taken a 2-1 lead in the series before Tampa Bay won three straight games. Caminero hit his first career postseason home run in the clincher, and closer Bryan Baker pitched the ninth inning to send the home crowd into celebration. Tampa Bay finished the regular season 98-64 and went 7-2 in the playoffs. The Guardians, who have not won a World Series since 1948, saw their run end in the ALCS.

History is on the line for both clubs. The Rays have played in the World Series twice before, losing to the Phillies four games to one in 2008 and to the Dodgers in six games in 2020. The Brewers and Rays are two of the five teams that have never won a World Series. It is also the first time the two teams have met in the playoffs. Milwaukee won two of three regular-season meetings between March 30 and April 1 at American Family Field.

The teams are closely matched at home, where each went 55-26 in the regular season. One storyline that stands out is Freddy Peralta, now a Tampa Bay starter, facing his former teammates on the Brewers, according to the analytics site The Analyst.

The pitching matchup for Game 1 was expected to feature Jacob Misiorowski for Milwaukee, who went 16-5 with a 1.80 ERA in the regular season, and Drew Rasmussen for Tampa Bay, who went 16-5 with a 2.67 ERA, according to Sports Illustrated. Rasmussen was in line to start on regular rest after pitching Game 5 of the ALCS. MLB.com describes Misiorowski and Logan Henderson as a dynamic one-two punch at the top of Milwaukee's rotation and says the Brewers' bullpen has been dominant.

The series follows a 2-3-2 format. Milwaukee hosts Games 1 and 2 on October 23 and 24. The series then moves to Tropicana Field for Games 3 and 4 on October 26 and 27, with Game 5 on October 28 if it is needed. Games 6 and 7, if necessary, return to Milwaukee on October 30 and 31. October 25 and October 29 are scheduled off days. All games are broadcast on FOX, with ESPN Radio providing national radio coverage.

As general background, the World Series is a best-of-seven championship, so the first team to win four games takes the title. In the 2-3-2 format, the team with the better regular-season record hosts the first two games and, if the series goes the distance, the last two.

Whichever club prevails will end a long wait and claim a first championship, either in Milwaukee or in Tampa Bay.
